tasks.prompt: Order a spare parts and obsolescence strategy for critical treatment equipment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in British Columbia exposed by long lead times for critical parts under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: critical equipment listed through stocking and obsolescence actions in place.

cards.label: List critical equipment from the asset criticality ranking and the consequence of each one failing
For each item, record part lead times, supplier support status, and whether the model is still produced
Set stocking levels for parts whose lead time exceeds the tolerable outage for that equipment
Create an obsolescence watch list with a planned response for each item: stock, retrofit, or replace
Fund and order the highest risk parts and record their location and shelf life requirements
Review the watch list at each management review and after every supplier discontinuation notice

tasks.explanation: Spares strategy is driven by lead time against tolerable outage, and the obsolescence watch turns a supplier notice into a planned response instead of a crisis.

tasks.prompt: Order a stage gate process for capital project delivery.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta where projects have reached construction with unresolved scope questions under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: gates defined through the process applied and audited on live projects.

cards.label: Define the gates: need confirmed, options evaluated, design complete, ready to tender, ready to commission, and closed out
Set the evidence each gate requires, including operations sign off on operability at design gates
Assign a gatekeeper outside the project team who can hold a project at a gate
Require a gate review meeting with the evidence circulated in advance and decisions recorded
Allow a project to proceed only when its gate evidence is complete or its gaps are formally accepted with owners
Audit gate records on completed projects each year and tighten the evidence list where gaps caused trouble

tasks.explanation: Stage gates work because an independent gatekeeper can hold a project, and operations signs off operability before concrete makes the answer permanent.

tasks.prompt: Order a design review process for a major treatment project.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan building a new treatment train with an external design team under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review stages set through design comments closed before tender.

cards.label: Set review stages at concept, preliminary, and detailed design with named utility reviewers for each stage
Issue each design package with enough time for operators and maintainers to review it against plant experience
Review for operability: access, isolation, sampling points, chemical handling, winter operation, and maintainability
Log every comment with a disposition the designer must answer, and track the log openly
Hold a comment resolution meeting and close or escalate every item before the next stage proceeds
Freeze the design at tender and handle later changes only through the management of change process

tasks.explanation: Design review gives operators time and a tracked comment log, because the cheapest moment to fix an unworkable valve location is on paper.

tasks.prompt: Order the commissioning and handover of a new treatment process to operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba starting up a new ultraviolet and filtration train under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: construction complete through operations accepting the process with full records.

cards.label: Verify construction is complete against the design, with a deficiency list and a date for every item
Test equipment and controls dry and then wet, in sequence, recording every test result
Run the process on water to waste or recycle until quality results meet the acceptance values
Train operators on the new process and assess competence before anyone runs it alone
Transfer the records package: drawings, manuals, warranties, spares, and programmed set points
Accept the process into operations formally, with deficiencies, training gaps, and warranty dates recorded

tasks.explanation: Handover is a formal acceptance based on quality results, trained operators, and a complete records package, not the day the contractor leaves the site.

tasks.prompt: Order a construction phase water quality protection plan for work inside a live plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 plant in British Columbia expanding while the existing plant keeps supplying water under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: construction risks mapped through the plan closed out at project end.

cards.label: Map every construction activity that could affect source, process, or treated water quality in the live plant
Set physical separations, hygiene rules, and material controls for work near open process water
Define the sampling and inspection checks that run during construction and who can stop work on a quality concern
Brief every contractor worker on the quality rules before site access and record the briefing
Inspect compliance weekly and after any incident, and increase treated water sampling while high risk work is under way
Close the plan at project end with a final inspection and a record of every quality event and its resolution

tasks.explanation: Building inside a live plant treats construction as a quality hazard from the first day, with stop work authority and extra sampling while the risk is highest.

tasks.prompt: Order a procurement evaluation process for a major treatment equipment package.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta buying a major membrane equipment package under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: requirements written through the award recommendation documented.

cards.label: Write the requirements as performance duties and guaranteed values, with the evaluation criteria published in advance
Form an evaluation team that includes operations and maintenance, not only project and purchasing staff
Score technical compliance first and open pricing only for proposals that meet the technical standard
Check references and, for the leading proposal, visit an operating installation of the same equipment
Record the scoring, the reference findings, and the reasons for the recommendation in an evaluation report
Award on the documented recommendation and file the report for audit and for the post project evaluation

tasks.explanation: Procurement protects quality by scoring technical compliance before price is seen, and the documented report is what makes the award defensible later.

tasks.prompt: Order a contractor management program for work at treatment facilities.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan using many contractors across its treatment sites under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: contractor risks defined through performance reviewed and records closed.

cards.label: Define the work categories and the competence, insurance in general terms, and safety requirements for each one
Prequalify contractors against those requirements before they are invited to work at a treatment site
Orient every contractor worker to site hazards, quality protection rules, and emergency arrangements before work starts
Supervise high risk work with permits and spot checks by utility staff
Review each contractor performance at job end for quality, safety, and site care, and record the rating
Use the ratings in future selection and remove contractors whose performance endangers water quality or safety

tasks.explanation: Contractor management starts before arrival with prequalification and orientation, and ends with a recorded rating that shapes who is invited back.

tasks.prompt: Order a shutdown and tie in plan for connecting a new process to a live plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Manitoba tying a new clearwell and pump hall into the operating plant under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: shutdown window chosen through the plant returned to normal operation.

cards.label: Choose the shutdown window from demand records, picking the lowest demand period and confirming storage can carry the community
Write the step sequence for isolation, draining, tie in, disinfection, and refilling with a time for each step
Assign every step an owner and a checker, and stage all materials and fittings before the window opens
Brief all shifts and notify the community and the regulator contact in general terms as the plan requires
Execute the sequence, sample at the defined points, and return sections to service only on satisfactory results
Review the tie in the next day and record timing, quality results, and every lesson for the next shutdown

tasks.explanation: A tie in succeeds on preparation: storage carries the community, materials are staged, and each section returns to service on sample results.

tasks.prompt: Order a project risk register process for a multi year treatment program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia delivering a multi year treatment renewal program under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: risks identified through risks retired or realized with lessons recorded.

cards.label: Identify program risks with the delivery team: technical, source, weather, market, approval, and community risks
Score each risk for likelihood and impact and name an owner who can act on it
Write a response for each major risk: avoid, reduce, transfer in general terms, or accept with a contingency
Fund contingencies for the accepted major risks and protect them from routine scope growth
Review the register monthly, retire risks whose window has passed, and add new ones as the program learns
At program close, record which risks materialized and how the responses performed, for the next program

tasks.explanation: A risk register earns its keep when contingencies are protected and the register is reviewed monthly, not when it is written once for the funding application.

tasks.prompt: Order a lessons learned program across capital projects.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta repeating the same design and start up mistakes across projects under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: capture points set through lessons verified in later projects.

cards.label: Set capture points at design freeze, commissioning, and one year after start up for every major project
Collect lessons from operators and maintainers as well as the project team, in their own words
Convert each significant lesson into a change to a standard, a checklist, or a specification clause
Assign each change an owner and verify the revised document is issued
Require the next project team to state how it applied the current lessons at its design gate
Review the lesson log yearly and retire lessons that practice has fully absorbed

tasks.explanation: Lessons are learned only when they change a standard and the next project must show how it used them, otherwise they are just stories told at close out.

tasks.prompt: Order an operability review for a plant expansion at the concept stage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan testing expansion concepts before design money is spent under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: concepts described through the preferred concept carried into design with conditions.

cards.label: Describe each expansion concept in operating terms: staffing, chemicals, residuals, energy, and winter behaviour
Have senior operators work each concept through normal, peak, failure, and maintenance scenarios on paper
Score each concept for operability and resilience as well as capacity and capital cost in general terms
Identify concept changes that remove operability problems while changes are still cheap
Recommend the preferred concept with its operating conditions and unresolved questions stated
Carry the conditions into the design brief so the concept operability findings cannot be lost

tasks.explanation: Operability review at concept stage is the cheapest review there is, because a concept that cannot be run in winter can be changed with a pencil.

tasks.prompt: Order an emergency response plan overhaul for a drinking water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Manitoba rewriting a plan that no longer matches its plants under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: hazards reassessed through the new plan exercised and adopted.

cards.label: Reassess the hazards the plan must cover: source contamination, treatment failure, power loss, flood, fire, cyber, and severe winter events
For each hazard, write the first hour actions, the decision authority, and the notifications in general terms
Rebuild the contact lists, mutual aid references, and resource inventories from current records
Set the plan format so a stressed operator can find the right section in the dark, in print and offline
Exercise the draft plan in a tabletop with the people who would actually lead each event
Correct the plan from the exercise, adopt it at leadership level, and set its review and exercise cycle

tasks.explanation: An emergency plan is written for the worst hour, not the office: it must be findable offline, led by named authority, and proven in an exercise before it is adopted.

tasks.prompt: Order a utility emergency exercise program, from tabletop to full scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia building staff readiness across its treatment sites under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: exercise needs assessed through findings tracked into the emergency plan.

cards.label: Assess which scenarios staff have never practised and which practised ones still produced confusion
Schedule a progression: discussion exercises first, then functional drills, then a full scale exercise
Write each scenario with injects that force real decisions, including a complication that arrives mid exercise
Run the exercise with evaluators who record decisions and times rather than helping the players
Debrief within days and convert every significant finding into a plan, training, or equipment action with an owner
Track the actions to completion and retest the weakest scenario in the next exercise cycle

tasks.explanation: Exercises build readiness in progression and are judged by tracked corrective actions, because a debrief that changes nothing trains people that findings do not matter.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership sequence for a boil water advisory decision.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta facing treated water results that may require a public advisory under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: results confirmed through the advisory lifted on evidence and communicated clearly.

cards.label: Confirm the results with repeat sampling and laboratory verification, and check treatment and distribution evidence at the same time
Convene the senior decision group and the health authority contact in general terms to assess the risk together
Decide on the advisory and its area from the confirmed evidence, recording the basis for the decision
Issue clear public instructions on what to do, who is affected, and where updates will appear, through every channel the community uses
Increase sampling across the affected area and correct the underlying cause while the advisory is in place
Lift the advisory only when the agreed evidence in general terms shows the water is safe, and communicate the lifting as widely as the issuing

tasks.explanation: Advisory leadership confirms before it alarms, decides with the health authority, and lifts on evidence communicated as loudly as the warning itself.

tasks.prompt: Order the leadership response to a major treatment plant outage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan whose largest plant is out of service after a major equipment failure under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: outage declared through normal service restored and reviewed.

cards.label: Declare the outage level, open the incident structure, and name the incident lead and the operations lead
Establish how long storage and the remaining plants can supply the community and set demand measures to match
Notify the governing body, the health and provincial contacts in general terms, and the community with honest time estimates
Direct the repair or bypass plan with safety and quality gates that cannot be traded for speed
Restore production in stages, returning water to service only on satisfactory quality results at each stage
Close the incident with a review that records decisions, timelines, and the resilience actions that follow

tasks.explanation: Outage leadership protects two clocks at once: the storage clock that limits supply, and the quality gate that no repair deadline is allowed to overrule.

tasks.prompt: Order the response leadership for a source water contamination incident.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba learning of a spill upstream of its river intake under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: report received through the source returned to normal use on evidence.

cards.label: Get the facts on the contaminant, quantity, location, and travel time from the reporting agency and verify them directly
Decide on intake closure, reduced rate, or continued use from the travel time and the treatment barrier evidence
Fill storage while the decision window allows and prepare the alternate source or supply arrangements
Increase source and treated sampling for the contaminant and for treatment performance indicators
Communicate with the health authority and the community in general terms on what is known, what is being done, and what residents should do
Return the intake to normal use only on sampling evidence and a documented leadership decision

tasks.explanation: Source incidents are won in the travel time window: facts first, storage filled early, and the intake reopens on evidence rather than on the spill fading from the news.

tasks.prompt: Order a cyber incident response process for treatment control systems.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia discovering suspicious activity on its treatment control network under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: suspicion reported through systems restored and lessons adopted.

cards.label: Train operators to report suspicious control behaviour immediately and to keep the plant in a safe manual state
Isolate the affected control segments from external connections while preserving local control and records
Convene the incident lead, control specialists, and leadership, and notify the required contacts in general terms
Operate the plant manually on verified local instruments until control systems are trusted again
Restore systems from known good backups in stages, verifying control and alarm behaviour at each stage
Review the incident, harden the weaknesses it exposed, and record the new controls in the security program

tasks.explanation: Cyber response in a treatment plant puts safe manual operation first and restores automation in verified stages, because water quality cannot wait for the network investigation.

tasks.prompt: Order a mutual aid agreement program with neighbouring utilities.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional group of western Canadian utilities in Alberta formalizing how they help each other under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: needs and offers mapped through agreements exercised and kept current.

cards.label: Map what each utility could need in an emergency and what it could offer: operators, equipment, laboratory capacity, and treated water in general terms
Agree the terms in advance: request process, cost handling in general terms, liability in general terms, and worker credentials
Sign the agreements at leadership level and file the contact and resource lists where incident leads can reach them
Brief senior staff on how to request and how to offer aid, and enter the process in the emergency plan
Exercise a mutual aid request in a joint drill, including travel and site orientation for the responding crew
Review the agreements yearly and after every real activation, updating resources and contacts

tasks.explanation: Mutual aid works when terms, credentials, and contacts are settled before the emergency, and a joint drill proves the paperwork can actually move people and equipment.

tasks.prompt: Order a power outage resilience program for treatment plants.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan where winter storms regularly interrupt grid power under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: critical loads defined through generation and fuel arrangements proven by test.

cards.label: Define the critical loads that must keep running: disinfection, controls, minimum pumping, heating, and communications
Size standby generation for those loads with the coldest start conditions in mind
Set fuel storage and resupply arrangements that cover the longest credible outage in winter road conditions
Write the load shedding sequence for non critical loads and the restart sequence when power returns
Test generation under real load on a set schedule, including a winter test, and correct every failure found
Record run performance and review the program after every real outage

tasks.explanation: Power resilience is proven by loaded winter tests, not by nameplate ratings, because a generator that has never carried the plant in January is a hope, not a barrier.

tasks.prompt: Order a wildfire watershed response program for a forest source utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia drawing from a forested watershed with rising fire risk under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: fire risk monitored through post fire source recovery managed over seasons.

cards.label: Monitor fire danger and watershed fire reports through the season and assign a staff watch during high danger periods
Pre plan treatment responses for ash, turbidity, and organics surges, with chemical and filter capacity staged
Set intake and storage actions for an approaching fire, including filling storage while source quality is still good
During and after a fire, increase source and treated sampling and adjust treatment on the pre planned responses
Assess burned slopes for erosion risk and work with land managers on mitigation that protects the intake
Track source recovery over the following seasons and keep the enhanced monitoring until trends return to the normal range

tasks.explanation: Wildfire response starts before the fire with staged treatment capacity and full storage, and it continues for seasons because burned watersheds keep delivering sediment long after the smoke clears.

tasks.prompt: Order a drought and low source level response program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional prairie utility in Alberta facing a multi year drought on its reservoir source under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: drought indicators set through demand and supply actions staged by trigger.

cards.label: Set drought indicators: reservoir level and inflow, source quality changes, and community demand trends
Define staged triggers with the supply and demand actions each stage starts, agreed with the governing body in advance
Model how long storage lasts at each stage under the driest recorded sequence, with quality effects included
Prepare the public communication for each stage so messages are ready before they are needed
Activate stages on the indicators, not on opinion, and record the decisions and their effects
Review the program after the drought breaks and revise the triggers from what the indicators actually showed

tasks.explanation: Drought programs act on pre agreed triggers and storage modelling, so hard decisions are made by the plan the governing body already accepted, not improvised under pressure.

tasks.prompt: Order the establishment of a performance benchmarking program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Saskatchewan joining a structured comparison with peer utilities under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: measures chosen through benchmarking repeated on a fixed cycle.

cards.label: Choose a small set of measures that leadership will actually act on: quality, reliability, energy, chemical use, and cost in general terms
Define each measure precisely, including boundaries and data sources, so peer numbers mean the same thing
Validate the utility own data for one year before comparing it with anyone else
Compare with peers of similar source, size, and climate, and investigate the largest gaps in both directions
Adopt improvement actions from the gaps where the peer evidence shows a better method, not only a better number
Repeat the cycle on a fixed schedule and report movement against the utility own past as well as the peers

tasks.explanation: Benchmarking improves a utility when definitions match and gaps lead to adopted methods, not when it produces a league table nobody acts on.

tasks.prompt: Order the design of a key performance indicator framework for treatment operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba replacing dozens of unused reports with a focused indicator set under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: leadership questions listed through indicators reviewed and pruned yearly.

cards.label: List the questions leadership must answer monthly about quality, reliability, efficiency, and risk
Select one or two indicators per question, favouring leading indicators that warn before quality is affected
Define each indicator with its formula, data source, owner, target, and the action a bad result triggers
Automate the data collection where possible so the set survives busy months
Publish the first scorecard and have leadership use it in a real review before adding any new indicator
Review the framework yearly and retire indicators that never changed a decision

tasks.explanation: An indicator earns its place by changing decisions: each one carries a target, an owner, and a defined action, or it leaves the scorecard.

tasks.prompt: Order an energy benchmarking and optimization program for treatment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia with rising energy use per treated volume under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: energy baseline built through verified savings adopted in operations.

cards.label: Meter or allocate energy by process for a representative year and calculate energy per treated volume by season
Benchmark against the utility own history and peer ranges, separating cold season effects from true inefficiency
Rank the saving opportunities that carry no quality risk, such as scheduling, sequencing, and off peak operation
Trial the largest opportunity with quality monitoring and compare energy at matched flows and temperatures
Adopt proven measures into operating procedures and train all shifts on them
Trend energy per volume monthly and investigate any month that breaks the improved pattern

tasks.explanation: Energy programs compare at matched flow and temperature, because winter will otherwise be credited or blamed for what operating practice actually did.

tasks.prompt: Order a chemical use benchmarking and reduction program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta comparing chemical use across its plants and seasons under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: use normalized through proven reductions adopted with quality protected.

cards.label: Normalize chemical use per treated volume and per unit of raw quality load for each plant and season
Identify where use is highest after normalization and check delivered dose accuracy there first
Run jar and plant trials at the high use sites to find the lowest dose that holds every quality target
Confirm residuals production and filter performance can sustain the trial doses
Adopt the proven doses as plant dose tables with raw quality based adjustment rules
Trend normalized use quarterly and repeat the trial cycle at the next highest use site

tasks.explanation: Chemical benchmarking normalizes for raw quality before judging a plant, and reductions are adopted only after residuals and filters prove they can live with them.

tasks.prompt: Order a monthly performance scorecard and review routine for senior leadership.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility leadership team in Saskatchewan instituting a disciplined monthly review under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: scorecard defined through actions tracked to the next review.

cards.label: Define a one page scorecard: quality, incidents, production, energy, chemical use, maintenance, and open risks
Set the data cut off and the owners who certify each figure before the meeting
Hold the review on a fixed day with the scorecard circulated in advance, and spend meeting time on variances and decisions
Record every decision with an owner and a due date in the action log during the meeting
Open the next review with the action log, closing completed actions and escalating overdue ones
Review the scorecard itself twice a year so it keeps matching the risks the utility actually faces

tasks.explanation: A monthly routine works when the figures are certified before the meeting and the next meeting opens with the last meeting actions, so nothing decided quietly disappears.

tasks.prompt: Order a continuous improvement program for treatment operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Manitoba wanting improvement owned by operators, not only by projects under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: improvement intake opened through results shared and the cycle repeated.

cards.label: Open a visible intake for improvement ideas from every shift, with a promise that each idea gets an answer
Screen ideas quickly for quality and safety risk and select a small number for active trials
Give each selected idea an owner, a trial period, and success measures agreed before the trial starts
Run the trials and judge them on the agreed measures, with quality data reviewed by the laboratory
Adopt successful trials into procedures and training, and thank and credit the originators publicly
Report the program results quarterly, including trials that were stopped, and open the next intake round

tasks.explanation: Continuous improvement survives when every idea gets an answer and stopped trials are reported honestly, because staff judge the program by what happens to their ideas.

tasks.prompt: Order an operational optimization audit cycle for a large plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large plant in British Columbia auditing its own optimization every two years under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: audit scope set through improvements verified at the next audit.

cards.label: Set the audit scope across process control, energy, chemicals, maintenance practice, and data quality
Collect a season of trend data for each area before the audit team arrives on the floor
Have auditors from another utility plant or a fresh internal team observe operation and test the trends against practice
Rank the findings by quality risk and by value, and agree the facts with plant staff
Convert the top findings into funded actions with owners in the improvement program
Verify the actions at the next audit and carry forward any that did not deliver their expected effect

tasks.explanation: An optimization audit pairs outside eyes with a season of trend data, and its findings live or die at the next audit when delivery is checked.

tasks.prompt: Order a data quality program for operational and laboratory data.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta whose decisions are undermined by inconsistent plant data under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: critical data listed through data quality reported with the scorecard.

cards.label: List the critical data the utility decides on: flows, levels, quality results, chemical use, and energy
Set a quality rule for each data set: range checks, calibration status, completeness, and a named data owner
Audit the current data against the rules and correct instruments, calculations, and entry practices at the source
Build automatic flags for out of range, missing, and stale values in the reporting system
Require data owners to explain flagged data in the monthly review rather than silently adjusting it
Report data completeness and flag counts on the scorecard so data quality stays visible to leadership

tasks.explanation: Data quality is fixed at the instrument and the entry practice, not in the spreadsheet, and visible flag counts keep leadership from deciding on numbers nobody trusts.

tasks.prompt: Order a peer utility comparison study on treatment practice.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan arranging structured exchanges with two similar cold climate utilities under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: partners and topics chosen through adopted practices verified at home.

cards.label: Choose peer utilities with similar source, processes, and climate, and agree the exchange topics and confidentiality in general terms
Prepare the utility own data and practice summaries honestly, including the areas it is weakest in
Host and visit in turn, with operators and maintainers in the room, not only managers
Record every practice difference and judge which ones would work under local source, staffing, and winter conditions
Trial the most promising adopted practice on a defined scale with success measures
Report the study outcomes to leadership and file the comparison as a reference for the next study cycle

tasks.explanation: Peer comparison works when weaknesses are shared honestly and borrowed practices are trialled locally, because a method that thrives in one plant can fail in another climate.

tasks.prompt: Order a plant water use and process efficiency audit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba where in plant water use has crept up over several years under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plant water balance built through reductions adopted and trended.

cards.label: Build a plant water balance: raw intake, treated output, backwash, residuals, flushing, and unaccounted volumes
Meter or estimate each in plant use for a representative month in each season
Find the largest uses and check them against their design purpose, including backwash triggers and durations
Trial reductions on the largest use first, such as quality based backwash triggers, with treated quality monitored
Adopt proven reductions into procedures and set a plant water use target by season
Trend the balance quarterly and investigate any quarter where unaccounted volume grows

tasks.explanation: A plant water balance finds efficiency in backwash and residuals practice, and every reduction is proven against treated quality before it becomes the target.

tasks.prompt: Order a winter operations readiness program at utility scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba preparing all its plants for a prairie winter under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: winter risks listed by plant through readiness confirmed before freeze up.

cards.label: List winter risks by plant: intake icing, frozen lines and instruments, access, chemical delivery, and staffing in storms
Inspect and test the protections for each risk: heat trace, insulation, backup heat, and winter chemical storage
Stock winter critical spares, chemicals, and fuel before freeze up, based on the longest credible delivery delay
Set winter operating rules: flux and loading limits, sampling adjustments, and visit frequency for unstaffed sites in severe weather
Brief all shifts on the winter rules and run a cold snap scenario exercise in the fall
Confirm readiness plant by plant in a leadership review before freeze up and close every open item with an owner and a date

tasks.explanation: Winter readiness is confirmed before freeze up with protections tested and stocks in place, because January is the worst month to discover what October should have fixed.

tasks.prompt: Order a cold climate treatment operating strategy for a utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in northern Alberta where water sits near freezing for five months under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: cold effects quantified through seasonal rules adopted and reviewed yearly.

cards.label: Quantify cold effects on the utility processes: coagulation, settling, filtration, membranes, disinfection, and chemical handling
Set cold season process targets and dose rules from plant data and jar work done at winter temperatures
Adjust loading and flux limits for the cold season so quality margins survive the slowest kinetics
Protect chemical systems against freezing and viscosity change, including feed line and storage heating checks
Schedule the changeover to cold rules on temperature triggers, not calendar dates, and brief all shifts
Review cold season performance each spring and revise the rules from the winter record

tasks.explanation: Cold strategy is built on winter temperature jar work and temperature triggers, because cold water chemistry does not follow the summer dose table or the calendar.

tasks.prompt: Order an intake icing management program for a river source utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan troubled by frazil ice at its river intake under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: icing history analysed through the program proven over a winter.

cards.label: Analyse icing history against river temperature, flow, wind, and the intake configurations in use at the time
Install or verify monitoring that warns of icing conditions: water temperature near freezing, intake differential, and screen condition
Set the response ladder: rate changes, screen cleaning methods, heat or air systems where fitted, and alternate intake use
Stage the equipment and staffing the highest response level needs, including safe access in the dark and in storms
Operate the ladder through the icing season and log every event with conditions and the response that worked
Review the season log and upgrade the weakest response step before the next winter

tasks.explanation: Frazil ice is managed on monitored warning signs and a practised response ladder, because by the time an intake is blocked the easy options have already passed.

tasks.prompt: Order a spring runoff readiness program for a prairie source utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba facing extreme turbidity and organics during spring melt under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: runoff forecast reviewed through the plant returned to normal rules on evidence.

cards.label: Review snowpack, soil moisture, and forecast melt timing with the source monitoring team
Pre run jar tests on the expected runoff quality range and set the runoff dose tables in advance
Build chemical, residuals handling, and filter capacity for the peak weeks, including overtime rosters
Set the trigger that moves the plant to runoff rules: raw turbidity, colour, or rate of change, whichever comes first
Operate on runoff rules with increased settled and filtered sampling until raw quality returns to the normal range
Close the season with a review of peak values, chemical use, and filter performance, and update the readiness program

tasks.explanation: Runoff readiness is built before the melt, with dose tables and residuals capacity ready, so the plant meets the worst water of the year with a plan instead of a scramble.

tasks.prompt: Order a climate adaptation assessment for treatment infrastructure.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia assessing flood, fire, drought, and freeze risks to its plants under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: climate hazards screened through adaptation actions placed in the capital plan.

cards.label: Screen the climate hazards for each site using regional projections in general terms: flood, wildfire, drought, extreme cold, and storm intensity
Test each plant against the hazards: which elevations flood, which sources shrink, which access roads fail first
Identify the adaptations for the highest risks, from raising equipment to source diversification in general terms
Sequence the adaptations with the renewal program so assets are adapted when they are replaced, not twice
Place the funded adaptations in the capital plan with their risk reduction stated
Review the assessment on a set cycle and after any extreme event that tests its assumptions

tasks.explanation: Adaptation is cheapest when it rides on renewal, so the assessment sequences protection with replacement and is retested after every real extreme event.

tasks.prompt: Order a freeze protection audit for unstaffed treatment sites.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta responsible for several small unstaffed treatment sites under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: sites inventoried through protections proven in a cold snap test.

cards.label: Inventory every unstaffed site with its water lines, instruments, chemicals, and heating systems
Walk each site before winter and test heat trace, heaters, insulation, and low temperature alarms by simulating a failure
Correct every failed protection and record the as found and as left condition with photographs
Set alarm response rules that account for winter travel time, including who attends and what they carry
Install or verify remote temperature and intrusion monitoring where a freeze could run undetected for days
Repeat the audit yearly and after any freeze event, and trend freeze alarms by site

tasks.explanation: Freeze protection at unstaffed sites is proven by simulated failure before winter, because the first real test otherwise comes at minus thirty with a two hour drive.

tasks.prompt: Order a seasonal staffing and coverage plan for extreme weather periods.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan whose plants must stay covered through blizzards and floods under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: coverage risks mapped through the plan tested in a weather exercise.

cards.label: Map which roles must be on site, which can work remotely, and which sites can run unstaffed for a defined period
Identify single person dependencies and the travel routes most likely to be cut by storms or flooding
Build storm rosters with staff who live near each plant, rest provisions, and on site supplies for extended stays
Set the activation triggers and the authority that calls the storm roster into effect
Brief all staff before the season and confirm contact and availability information is current
Test the plan in a weather scenario exercise and correct the coverage gaps it exposes

tasks.explanation: Extreme weather coverage is planned around who can actually reach the plant, with rest and supplies for long stays, and it is exercised before the storm does the testing.

tasks.prompt: Order a source water protection program leadership review for a utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia leading a multi partner source protection program under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: protection plan actions reviewed through priorities reset with partners.

cards.label: Collect the status of every source protection action and the monitoring evidence on source quality trends
Review new land use, spill, and development pressures in the watershed since the last review
Assess which protection actions are delivering measurable risk reduction and which are stalled
Reprioritize the program with the watershed partners, assigning owners and dates for the next period
Report the review to utility leadership and the partners, including any risk the program cannot control
Set the monitoring or treatment contingency for uncontrolled risks and record it in the quality strategy

tasks.explanation: Source protection leadership admits which risks the program cannot control and covers those with monitoring and treatment contingencies, instead of reporting activity as if it were protection.

tasks.prompt: Order a watershed monitoring program design for a utility source.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta designing monitoring that gives early warning for its reservoir and tributaries under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: warning questions defined through the program reviewed after its first year.

cards.label: Define the decisions the monitoring must support: intake changes, treatment readiness, and source protection actions
Select parameters and stations that answer those decisions, favouring continuous instruments where warning time matters
Set sampling frequencies and storm event sampling so the program captures the conditions that drive treatment risk
Assign data review duties with thresholds that trigger a call to the plant, not only a filed report
Run the program for a first year and check which stations and parameters actually changed a decision
Revise the program from the first year evidence and file the design basis with the source protection plan

tasks.explanation: Watershed monitoring is designed backwards from decisions and warning time, and stations that never change a decision are moved or retired.

tasks.prompt: Order a winter chemical delivery and storage assurance program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba dependent on long winter supply routes for treatment chemicals under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: supply routes mapped through winter stocks verified monthly.

cards.label: Map each critical chemical from supplier to plant, including route, carrier, and the winter failure points
Set minimum winter stock levels from the longest credible delivery interruption for each chemical
Agree contingency arrangements with suppliers and neighbouring utilities in general terms before winter
Raise stocks to winter levels before freeze up and verify tank condition and heating for freeze sensitive chemicals
Track stock against the winter minimum weekly through the season and escalate early when a delivery slips
Review the program each spring and adjust minimums from the interruptions that actually occurred

tasks.explanation: Winter chemical assurance sets stock from the longest credible interruption and escalates on the first slipped delivery, while options still exist.

tasks.prompt: Order a workforce competency and certification assurance program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Saskatchewan assuring every critical task is covered by a competent operator under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: critical tasks listed through competence verified and gaps closed.

cards.label: List the critical tasks by plant and the competence and certification each task requires in general terms
Assess every operator against the list using records, supervised practice, and supervisor confirmation
Build the coverage matrix and mark tasks with fewer than two competent operators as risks
Create development plans for the gaps, with training, mentoring, and supervised practice scheduled
Restrict uncovered critical tasks to competent staff until the development plans close the gaps
Review the matrix quarterly and report single person risks to leadership until they are resolved

tasks.explanation: Competency assurance counts coverage, not certificates alone: a critical task with one competent operator is a recorded risk until a second person can do it.

tasks.prompt: Order a succession plan for senior operator and utility leadership roles.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba where several senior staff are near retirement under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: critical roles identified through readiness reviewed yearly.

cards.label: Identify the roles whose sudden vacancy would endanger quality, compliance in general terms, or supply
Record the knowledge each role holds that exists nowhere else: source behaviour, plant quirks, contacts, and history
Capture that knowledge in procedures, records, and structured mentoring before it is needed
Name at least one developing successor per role and build a readiness plan with acting opportunities
Let successors act in the role during planned absences with the incumbent reachable but not directing
Review readiness yearly and after every acting period, and adjust the plans from what the acting periods revealed

tasks.explanation: Succession is proven by acting periods, not by names on a chart, and unique knowledge is captured while its holder is still there to teach it.

tasks.prompt: Order an operator training program design for a multi plant utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia standardizing training across plants of different sizes under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: training needs analysed through the program evaluated and revised yearly.

cards.label: Analyse training needs from the competency matrix, incident lessons, audit findings, and upcoming process changes
Design the program in layers: plant induction, process specific training, emergency practice, and continuing development
Set the delivery mix of supervised practice, classroom, and online study so hands on skills are practised, not only described
Schedule training so every shift gets equal access and no plant loses coverage to attend
Assess learning by observed practice and questioning, and record competence separately from attendance
Evaluate the program yearly against incidents and audit findings and revise the content that is not changing practice

tasks.explanation: Training is evaluated by changed practice and fewer repeated incidents, and attendance records alone are never accepted as evidence of competence.

tasks.prompt: Order a safety management program review for treatment operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Alberta reviewing its safety program after several near misses under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program elements reviewed through corrective actions verified in the field.

cards.label: Review the program elements: hazard assessment, procedures, training, inspections, incident reporting, and contractor safety
Compare reported near misses and incidents with inspection findings to find hazards the system is missing
Walk the plants with operators and record the hazards they manage daily that no document mentions
Rank the program gaps by injury risk and assign each one an owner and a corrective action
Implement the actions, updating procedures and training where the gap was systemic
Verify the fixes in the field after a set period and report the review outcomes to all staff

tasks.explanation: A safety review trusts the plant floor over the filing cabinet: hazards operators manage silently every day are the program gaps that matter most.

tasks.prompt: Order a chemical safety and handling program upgrade for a utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan upgrading chlorine and bulk chemical safety across its plants under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: chemical hazards inventoried through drills proving the upgraded program.

cards.label: Inventory every chemical by plant with quantities, hazards, storage condition, and emergency equipment status
Compare storage, containment, ventilation, and handling practice with current safety guidance in general terms
Correct the highest risk gaps first, including leak response equipment and eyewash and shower access
Rewrite the handling and delivery procedures with the operators who do the work, and train every affected shift
Run a chemical release drill at the highest risk plant and record response times and equipment performance
Set the inspection and drill cycle and report program status at each management review

tasks.explanation: Chemical safety upgrades are sequenced by risk and proven by a release drill, because equipment that has never been used in a drill may not work in an emergency.

tasks.prompt: Order a laboratory quality system management program for a utility laboratory.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility laboratory in Manitoba strengthening the system behind its treated water results under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: methods and quality checks inventoried through the system audited and improved.

cards.label: Inventory the methods in use, their quality checks, and the analysts authorized for each method
Set the quality control rules: blanks, duplicates, spikes, and control limits, with the actions a failed check triggers
Schedule calibrations, proficiency samples in general terms, and method reviews so none lapse unnoticed
Require a documented review of every result batch before results are released for decisions
Audit the laboratory records and practices against the system rules with an auditor from outside the laboratory
Correct the audit findings and trend quality control performance at the utility management review

tasks.explanation: Laboratory quality rests on rules that stop bad results from being released, and on outside audit, because a laboratory grading only itself will eventually believe itself.

tasks.prompt: Order a sampling quality assurance program for field sampling.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia whose field samples support major treatment decisions under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: sampling error sources listed through sampler competence verified yearly.

cards.label: List the error sources in field sampling: location, timing, containers, preservation, transport, and documentation
Standardize the sampling procedures with photographs of correct technique at the real sampling points
Train samplers and verify technique by observed sampling and by field blank and duplicate results
Set the field quality sample rate and the acceptance review every batch of field results receives
Investigate out of pattern field quality results to their source and retrain or repair as the evidence directs
Review field quality performance yearly and report it with the laboratory quality results

tasks.explanation: Field sampling quality is verified by observed technique and by blanks and duplicates, because the best laboratory cannot repair a badly taken sample.

tasks.prompt: Order a mentorship program pairing senior and developing operators.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta formalizing how its senior operators develop the next generation under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: pairings made through the program reviewed and renewed yearly.

cards.label: Select mentors for demonstrated judgement and teaching ability, not only for years of service
Pair each developing operator with a mentor outside their direct reporting line where possible
Set the pairing goals: specific processes, decisions, and emergency scenarios the mentee must work through
Schedule regular plant time together, including at least one difficult operating period such as runoff or a cold snap
Have the mentee lead real tasks under observation and review the decisions together afterwards
Review each pairing at six months, record progress against the goals, and renew or change pairings yearly

tasks.explanation: Mentorship transfers judgement through real decisions in hard operating periods, reviewed afterwards, which no classroom can replicate.

tasks.prompt: Order a fatigue and shift work management review for continuous operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan reviewing rosters at plants that run around the clock under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: roster risks assessed through revised rosters monitored for effect.

cards.label: Assess current rosters for consecutive nights, short changeovers, overtime load, and single coverage periods
Gather operator experience of fatigue honestly, including commute risks after night shifts in winter
Compare roster options against current guidance in general terms and against the coverage the plants require
Trial the preferred roster with overtime and incident monitoring for a full rotation cycle
Adopt the roster that holds coverage with the lowest fatigue risk and set overtime limits with escalation rules
Monitor fatigue indicators, incidents, and overtime at the monthly review and adjust the roster if risk creeps back

tasks.explanation: Fatigue management treats the roster as a safety control, trials changes over a full cycle, and keeps monitoring because overtime creep quietly rebuilds the old risk.

tasks.prompt: Order an incident investigation program for quality and safety events.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Manitoba learning inconsistently from its incidents under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: investigation triggers set through lessons tracked across the utility.

cards.label: Set which events must be investigated: quality excursions, injuries, near misses with serious potential, and major equipment failures
Secure the facts first: records, samples, photographs, and operator accounts taken while memory is fresh
Analyse causes with a structured method that separates the immediate cause from the system causes behind it
Recommend actions aimed at the system causes, each with an owner, a due date, and a way to verify effect
Share the findings with every plant in the utility, not only the one where the event happened
Track the actions in the corrective action system and review investigation quality yearly

tasks.explanation: Investigations aim at system causes and share lessons utility wide, because the same latent weakness usually exists quietly at the other plants too.

tasks.prompt: Order an inspection readiness program for a provincial drinking water inspection.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta preparing for a routine provincial inspection in general terms under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: inspection scope anticipated through the plant ready and staff briefed.

cards.label: Review the findings and recommendations of the last inspection and confirm every one is closed with evidence
Walk the plant as an inspector would, checking records, labelling, sampling points, and process condition
Assemble the records an inspector is likely to request in general terms, indexed and complete for the review period
Brief operators on answering accurately and showing records, and on escalating questions they cannot answer
Correct the gaps the walk finds, prioritizing anything that affects treated water quality or record integrity
Hold a short readiness confirmation with leadership and file the preparation record with the inspection file

tasks.explanation: Inspection readiness is mostly closing the last inspection with evidence and walking the plant with an inspector eyes, long before the visit is announced.

tasks.prompt: Order a regulatory change management process for a drinking water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan tracking provincial and guideline changes in general terms under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: change sources monitored through changes implemented and verified.

cards.label: Assign an owner to monitor provincial requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality updates in general terms
Log each relevant change with its effective horizon and the processes, sampling, or records it touches
Assess the gap between the change and current practice with operations and laboratory staff
Build an implementation plan with owners, dates, training, and any capital needs the gap requires
Implement the changes and update procedures, sampling programs, and records before the effective date
Verify the implementation by audit and report readiness to leadership ahead of the deadline

tasks.explanation: Regulatory change is managed like any other change, with a gap assessment and a verified implementation, so a new requirement never arrives as a surprise.

tasks.prompt: Order an adverse water quality incident reporting and review process.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba standardizing how adverse results are reported and reviewed under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: adverse results defined through the process audited for timeliness and completeness.

cards.label: Define the adverse results and events that must be reported, the internal chain, and the external notifications in general terms
Set the reporting clock and the backup contacts so a result at night or on a holiday moves as fast as one at midday
Require the immediate corrective actions to be recorded with the report: resampling, treatment checks, and public protection steps
Review every adverse event at senior level for cause, response quality, and communication quality
Convert review findings into corrective actions in the utility corrective action system
Audit reporting timeliness and completeness yearly and retrain the chain where the audit finds delays

tasks.explanation: Adverse reporting is a timed chain that must work at night and on holidays, and every event is reviewed for response quality, not only for its cause.

tasks.prompt: Order a utility financial planning cycle for treatment operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia aligning its operating and capital budgets with its quality strategy under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: needs gathered through in year performance managed against the plan.

cards.label: Gather the needs from the quality strategy, asset condition, staffing plans, and the capital plan
Build the operating forecast by cost driver in general terms: chemicals, energy, labour, maintenance, and laboratory
Test the forecast against service levels and identify what must be deferred if funding falls short, with the risk of each deferral stated
Present the integrated operating and capital picture to the governing body for decision
Adopt the budgets and assign each major line a manager accountable for its delivery
Review performance against the plan quarterly and reforecast the year honestly when conditions change

tasks.explanation: Financial planning states the risk of every deferral beside its saving, so a budget decision is taken with its quality consequence visible.

tasks.prompt: Order a rate and affordability study process for drinking water services.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta studying how to fund its renewal program fairly over time under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: revenue needs defined through the adopted path reported against yearly.

cards.label: Define the revenue the operating plan and the twenty year capital plan require in general terms
Analyse how the current charges recover those needs across customer classes in general terms
Model gradual and stepped funding paths and their effects on reserves and on future charges
Assess affordability effects on the community and the options that soften them without underfunding renewal
Present the paths and their long term consequences to the governing body in plain language
Adopt a path, communicate it clearly to the community, and report progress against it every year

tasks.explanation: A rate study compares funding paths over decades and states consequences plainly, because deferring renewal is also a decision and its bill arrives with interest in failures.

tasks.prompt: Order a stakeholder and community engagement program for a major treatment upgrade.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan planning a visible multi year plant upgrade under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: affected groups mapped through engagement maintained through construction.

cards.label: Map the groups affected by the upgrade: neighbours, water users, Indigenous communities in general terms, businesses, and regulators in general terms
Learn each group concerns and preferred ways of being engaged before the project design is fixed
Share the project need, options, and effects honestly, including construction noise, traffic, and service interruptions
Record every commitment the engagement produces and assign each one an owner in the project team
Report back on how input changed the project and on the commitments as they are delivered
Keep the engagement running through construction with regular updates and a named contact for concerns

tasks.explanation: Engagement starts before the design is fixed and reports back on what input changed, because consultation after decisions are made is notification, not engagement.

tasks.prompt: Order a public communication program for routine water quality reporting.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba improving how it communicates quality results to its community under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: audience needs assessed through communication reviewed and improved yearly.

cards.label: Assess what the community actually asks about water quality from calls, complaints, and council questions
Set a plain language reporting routine: what is published, how often, and where, in accessible formats
Prepare explanations for the common concerns in advance, reviewed by operations and laboratory staff for accuracy
Train the staff who speak with the public so answers are consistent, honest about uncertainty, and free of jargon
Publish on schedule through good news and bad, including adverse results with the actions taken
Review reach and community feedback yearly and revise the program from what residents say they still do not understand

tasks.explanation: Public trust is built by publishing on schedule in plain language, including adverse results with their actions, not by communicating only when the news is good.

tasks.prompt: Order a board reporting and governance calendar for a water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility board in British Columbia professionalizing its oversight of drinking water operations under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: board information needs defined through the calendar reviewed after its first year.

cards.label: Define the information the board needs to govern: quality performance, risk, finance, major projects, and workforce, in general terms
Set an annual calendar that gives each topic a scheduled deep review instead of crowding every meeting
Standardize report formats so trends are comparable meeting to meeting and figures trace to source records
Require management to present options and recommendations, not only information, for every decision item
Record board decisions and directions in minutes that name owners and dates, and track them like management actions
Review the calendar and report quality with the board after the first year and adjust the topics and depth

tasks.explanation: Board governance improves when each risk gets a scheduled deep review and board directions are tracked with the same discipline as management actions.

tasks.prompt: Order a utility risk register and annual risk review at leadership level.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Alberta maintaining one register for its treatment risks under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: risks consolidated through the register driving plans and budgets.

cards.label: Consolidate risks from quality, assets, source, workforce, finance, cyber, and climate into one register with common scoring
Score each risk for likelihood and consequence and name the owner closest to the controls
Record the existing controls and judge honestly whether they reduce the risk or only describe it
Set a treatment action for every risk above the leadership tolerance, with funding identified
Review the register at leadership level twice a year and after any incident that changes a score
Use the top risks to shape the strategic plan, the capital plan, and the exercise program for the next year

tasks.explanation: One register with honest control judgements lets leadership compare a cyber risk with a source risk, and the top risks visibly shape the plans and budgets that follow.

tasks.prompt: A prairie city reviews its ultrafiltration fleet after one of four membrane halls shows rising chemical cleaning costs while the other three halls hold steady.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Hall 3 cleaning chemical use has doubled in a year while Halls 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged.
Normalized permeability in Hall 3 falls faster after each clean than in the other halls on the same feed.
Feed water quality, flux and temperature are common to all four halls and within normal ranges.
A fibre sample from Hall 3 shows heavy iron and manganese deposits, while samples from Hall 1 are clean.
Hall 3 is the only hall fed through an older raw water line where a corrosion study found tuberculation.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The whole membrane fleet is reaching end of life at the same time
Feed water quality has deteriorated for the entire plant
Cleaning chemical prices rose for all halls
Iron and manganese fouling specific to Hall 3, linked to its corroding feed line, is driving the cleaning costs

inference.explanation: Only Hall 3 differs, which rules out plant wide feed quality and fleet ageing. The metals deposits, the faster permeability loss and the corroded dedicated feed line all point one way.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived chemical supplier invoices for the whole plant
Archived membrane purchase dates for all halls
Archived Hall 3 feed line inspection and metals results compared with the other halls

nextClue.explanation: Archived Hall 3 feed line inspection and metals results compared with the other halls directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Invoices rose slightly for everyone, which does not explain why only Hall 3 cleaning doubled.
clueText.nc-b: All halls were installed in the same year, so age alone cannot split Hall 3 from the rest.
clueText.nc-c: Hall 3 feed samples carry far higher iron and manganese than the common header, and the line inspection shows heavy tuberculation.

tasks.prompt: A utility wide review finds free chlorine residuals collapsing at the far end of one pressure zone in a British Columbia system, while other zones hold target residuals.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Zone 4 residuals fall below target within two days of leaving the plant, while Zones 1 to 3 hold for five days.
Zone 4 contains the oldest cast iron mains in the system and the highest water age in the utility.
Plant effluent chlorine dose and residual leaving the plant are at target and unchanged.
A zone study found heavy pipe wall deposits and a high chlorine demand in Zone 4 samples.
Flushing Zone 4 mains restores residuals for about a week before they collapse again.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: A cross connection is diluting Zone 4 water
The Zone 4 sample taps are faulty
Pipe wall demand in the old Zone 4 mains is consuming the residual, not a plant dosing problem
The plant chlorine dose is too low for the whole system

inference.explanation: The plant dose is proven good by the zones that hold residual. Zone 4 alone combines the oldest mains, the highest water age and measured high wall demand, and flushing only buys a week, which fits wall demand regrowing.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived customer complaint log for Zone 4
Archived Zone 4 water age and pipe condition study with bench chlorine demand results
Archived plant chlorine dose records

nextClue.explanation: Archived Zone 4 water age and pipe condition study with bench chlorine demand results directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Complaints cluster on taste after flushing, which follows the demand problem rather than causing it.
clueText.nc-b: Bench tests on Zone 4 pipe sections show very high wall demand, and water age there is double the utility average.
clueText.nc-c: Plant dose records are at target, and other zones on the same water hold residuals for days.

tasks.prompt: A northern Alberta utility investigates why one of six dual media filters needs backwashing twice as often as its sisters after a raw water intake upgrade.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Filter 5 backwash frequency has doubled since the intake upgrade, while Filters 1 to 4 and 6 are unchanged.
The upgrade moved the intake to a deeper, colder layer with higher dissolved manganese.
Filter 5 is the only filter whose media was topped up with a finer sand than specified last year.
Headloss across Filter 5 builds in the top 150 mm of media, and core samples show a dense surface crust with manganese coating.
Filters on the same water with correct media grade show even headloss through the bed depth.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Filter 5 has a broken underdrain
The finer than specified top media on Filter 5 is trapping solids and manganese at the surface and blinding the bed
The new intake water is overloading every filter in the plant
The backwash system is undersized for the whole plant

inference.explanation: A shared water change cannot explain a single filter changing. The headloss sits at the surface, the crust is in the top layer, and that layer alone was replaced with off specification media.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived Filter 5 media specification and core sample gradation results
Archived intake water quality trend for the whole plant
Archived backwash pump capacity test

nextClue.explanation: Archived Filter 5 media specification and core sample gradation results directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Gradation testing confirms the top layer is far finer than specified and coated with manganese, matching the surface crust.
clueText.nc-b: Intake manganese rose for all filters, yet only Filter 5 changed behaviour, so the water alone is not the cause.
clueText.nc-c: Backwash capacity tests pass, and other filters clean fully on the same system.

tasks.prompt: A utility energy audit finds one of two identical raw water pump stations using 40 percent more energy per megalitre than its twin station on the same reservoir.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 4 water treatment utility case for study: records, bench tests, benchmarks and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Stations A and B have identical pumps, motors and duty points on paper and pump from the same reservoir.

Source management and blending with the deep wells is the supported strategy, with treatment held as a later option
Ion exchange treatment should be built immediately at full scale
The rising wells should be abandoned this year

inference.explanation: Eight years of rise rules out waiting. The aquifer split explains which wells rise, and blending is proven by modelling to buy a decade, so immediate full scale treatment or abandonment overshoots the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: The quote shows treatment is the costliest path and its brine has no local discharge route.
clueText.nc-b: Fertilizer sales do not change the measured well trends, which are the deciding record.
clueText.nc-c: The blending model holds finished water well below the guideline for a decade using existing wells.
